name: Liver detox for yellow sclera

card.summary: The belief that a liver cleanse can whiten yellowish eye whites; medical sources tie true yellowing to bilirubin and advise evaluation.
card.note: Yellow sclera can signal liver, blood or bile duct disease; no studies test detox regimens for eye whiteness.

quick.overview:
Some appearance-focused discussions hold that yellowish eye whites reflect a congested liver and can be cleared with a liver detox or cleanse. The practice is a belief about appearance rather than an established medical treatment.

Medical references describe yellowing of the white of the eye as scleral (conjunctival) icterus, a sign of raised bilirubin, which has liver, blood and bile duct causes.
quick.mechanism: Proponents link liver function to eye colour. In medical descriptions, bilirubin deposits in the conjunctiva, which binds it readily, and visible yellowing generally indicates serum bilirubin of about 3 mg/dL or more.
quick.risks: Because yellow eyes with yellow skin can accompany hepatitis, cirrhosis, haemolysis or bile duct obstruction, medical sources say it warrants evaluation. Detox products themselves have not been studied for this purpose.

lead: Liver detox for yellow sclera is the practice of using cleansing diets, herbs, supplements or home liver cleanses with the aim of whitening yellowish or dull eye whites and giving the eyes a brighter, healthier look. Followers connect eye-white colour to liver health, and bright, clear whites are widely associated with a rested, healthy appearance.

Medical sources describe yellowing of the white of the eye as scleral icterus, a sign of jaundice. The pigment deposits in the conjunctiva, which has a high affinity for bilirubin, so it can appear before skin yellowing; visible conjunctival icterus generally indicates serum bilirubin of at least about 3 mg/dL.[1] Causes are classed as prehepatic (excess red cell breakdown), hepatic (liver damage or inherited conjugation defects) and posthepatic (bile duct blockage).[1]

Wikipedia's article on the sclera notes that eye-white colour also varies with age, skin tone and other conditions: fatty deposits can make the whites look slightly yellow in older adults, darker skin can have naturally darker sclerae, and irritation can redden them.[2] No published study has tested a detox regimen for eye whiteness.

chain: Cleanse, herb or supplement regimen aimed at the liver
Proponents say bilirubin or liver load drops
Eye whites look whiter and brighter
angle.text: People who follow this idea hope that supporting the liver will clear yellowish tints and dullness from the eye whites, leaving brighter, clearer-looking eyes. Medical sources link true yellowing to bilirubin and recommend evaluation, as described below.

infobox: Serum bilirubin of about 3 mg/dL or more[1]

paras: Jaundice from high bilirubin usually involves the conjunctivae and diffuse yellowing of the skin. Carotenemia from large intakes of carotene-rich foods typically spares the conjunctivae and shows mainly on the palms and soles, and some drugs such as rifampin can yellow the skin without jaundice.[1] Gilbert syndrome, found in about 5% of people, involves a less efficient bilirubin-processing enzyme with otherwise normal liver function and usually mild, stress-related jaundice.[1] Medical references note that yellowing with yellow skin should be evaluated because it can signal liver, blood or bile duct disease.[1]

Wikipedia's article on the sclera adds that jaundice produces yellow or light green tint, that conjunctivitis reddens the whites, and that some conditions such as osteogenesis imperfecta give a bluish tint.[2]

Detox diets and cleanses are described by Wikipedia as aiming to remove unspecified "toxins" through fasting, restrictive eating, herbs or similar practices.[3] Proponents say these practices release stored toxins that are then expelled in blood, skin, urine or stool.[3] The article reports that scientists and health bodies consider the concept unsupported, that a 2015 review found no convincing evidence that detox diets remove toxins, and that the liver and kidneys are the body's own detoxification system.[3] It also lists documented harms from some regimens, including cases of kidney injury and risks of prolonged fasting.[3]

On T Nation, members discuss liver cleanses such as lemon juice and olive oil, and coffee enemas, with some users reporting benefits and others citing Mayo Clinic warnings about harm.[4][5] One user wrote that a lemon-and-olive-oil cleanse improved his eye allergy symptoms.[4]

lore.intro: Liver-cleanse discussions on T Nation mention eye and allergy changes in passing; yellow sclera specifically is rarely discussed.[4][5]

claims.claim: A liver cleanse whitens yellow eye whites.
claims.believers: Users of lemon-and-olive-oil cleanses describe improved eyes and fewer allergy symptoms afterward.[4]
claims.experts: Medical references tie true yellowing to elevated bilirubin from liver, blood or bile duct causes and advise evaluation; no study has tested cleanses for eye whiteness.[1]

claims.claim: Detox diets remove toxins and improve organ function.
claims.believers: Proponents say fasting and restriction release stored toxins.[3]
claims.experts: A 2015 review found no convincing evidence that detox diets remove toxins, and sources list harms from some regimens.[3]
